title: The Iron Law of Oligarchy
text:
In the early twentieth century the German Social Democratic Party was the largest and best organized socialist movement in Europe. It was committed to democracy and equality, and its members elected their leaders. The young sociologist Robert Michels, who had himself been active in socialist politics, set out to study how such parties and their allied trade unions actually worked.

What he found troubled him. As the organizations grew, they needed full-time officials, specialists and spokesmen. These leaders gained knowledge, skills, contacts and control over the party's newspapers and money that ordinary members lacked. Most members had little time or interest to follow party affairs closely and tended to defer to the experts. Once in office, leaders often stayed for many years, and their priority shifted toward preserving the organization and their own positions rather than pursuing its radical goals.

In his 1911 book Michels argued that this was not a failing of particular people but a tendency of all large organizations, even those founded on democratic ideals. He summed it up in a phrase that became famous: "Who says organization, says oligarchy." He called it the iron law of oligarchy.
lesson: Every organization tends to concentrate power in a few hands over time. Build in term limits, transparency and real ways for members to hold leaders to account.
source: Michels, R. (1911). Zur Soziologie des Parteiwesens in der modernen Demokratie. Klinkhardt. English translation: Political Parties (1915).
caveat: Later research found organizations that resisted the tendency for long periods, so most scholars treat it as a strong tendency rather than an iron law.
